  • All negative → 0.
  • The whole tree is a BST.
  • Duplicate values (not a BST).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space.

Hard 1932. Merge BSTs to Create Single BST Amazon Microsoft BSTHash Map

Problem: Given n small BSTs with distinct roots, repeatedly replace a leaf with the tree whose root has that value. Return the final BST if all merge into one valid BST, else None.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: trees = [[2,1],[3,2,5],[5,4]]
Output: [3,2,5,1,null,4]
Explanation: In the first operation, pick i=1 and j=0, and merge trees[0] into trees[1]. Delete trees[0], so trees = [[3,2,5,1],[5,4]]. In the second operation, pick i=0 and j=1, and merge trees[1] into trees[0]. Delete trees[1], so trees = [[3,2,5,1,null,4]]. The resulting tree, shown above, is a valid BST, so return its root.
Example 2
Input: trees = [[5,3,8],[3,2,6]]
Output: []
Explanation: Pick i=0 and j=1 and merge trees[1] into trees[0]. Delete trees[1], so trees = [[5,3,8,2,6]]. The resulting tree is shown above. This is the only valid operation that can be performed, but the resulting tree is not a valid BST, so return null.

Constraints: n == trees.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 5 * 10⁴ · The number of nodes in each tree is in the range [1, 3]. · Each node in the input may have children but no grandchildren. · No two roots of trees have the same value. · All the trees in the input are valid BSTs. · 1 ≤ TreeNode.val ≤ 5 * 10⁴.

Hint 1

Which tree's root must be the final root?

Hint 2

Attach trees at matching leaves during a DFS that also checks BST bounds.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying merge orders is exponential; the forced structure plus one validating DFS is linear.

Spot it: Each tree root can attach under exactly one matching leaf, so the final root is the only root that isn't a leaf value anywhere (a hash map of roots and a count of leaves). Then DFS from that root, replacing leaves from the map, and validate the BST with value bounds.

Why not another pattern? Trying merge orders is exponential; any order of valid attachments gives the same tree.

Approach:

  1. Map root value → tree; collect all leaf values.
  2. The final root is a tree whose root value isn't a leaf value (must be exactly one).
  3. DFS with bounds (lo, hi): a leaf matching a stored root is replaced by that tree (removing it from the map); fail if any value breaks the bounds.
  4. Succeed only if every tree was used.
class Solution:
    def canMerge(self, trees: List[TreeNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        roots = {t.val: t for t in trees}
        leaves = set()
        for t in trees:
            for child in (t.left, t.right):
                if child:
                    leaves.add(child.val)
        top = [t for t in trees if t.val not in leaves]
        if len(top) != 1:
            return None  # no unique final root
        root = top[0]
        del roots[root.val]

        def build(node, lo, hi):  # attach trees at leaves and check BST bounds
            if node is None:
                return True
            if not lo < node.val < hi:
                return False
            if node.left is None and node.right is None and node.val in roots:
                sub = roots.pop(node.val)  # replace this leaf with its tree
                node.left, node.right = sub.left, sub.right
            return build(node.left, lo, node.val) and build(node.right, node.val, hi)

        ok = build(root, float("-inf"), float("inf"))
        return root if ok and not roots else None  # every tree must be used
function canMerge(trees: Array<TreeNode | null>): TreeNode | null {
    const roots = new Map<number, TreeNode>();
    for (const t of trees) {
        roots.set(t!.val, t!);
    }
    const leaves = new Set<number>();
    for (const t of trees) {
        for (const child of [t!.left, t!.right]) {
            if (child !== null) {
                leaves.add(child.val);
            }
        }
    }
    const top = trees.filter((t) => !leaves.has(t!.val));
    if (top.length !== 1) {
        return null;  // no unique final root
    }
    const root = top[0]!;
    roots.delete(root.val);

    // attach trees at leaves and check BST bounds
    function build(node: TreeNode | null, lo: number, hi: number): boolean {
        if (node === null) {
            return true;
        }
        if (!(lo < node.val && node.val < hi)) {
            return false;
        }
        if (node.left === null && node.right === null && roots.has(node.val)) {
            const sub = roots.get(node.val)!;  // replace this leaf with its tree
            roots.delete(node.val);
            node.left = sub.left;
            node.right = sub.right;
        }
        return build(node.left, lo, node.val) && build(node.right, node.val, hi);
    }

    const ok = build(root, -Infinity, Infinity);
    return ok && roots.size === 0 ? root : null;  // every tree must be used
}
class Solution {
    private Map<Integer, TreeNode> roots;

    public TreeNode canMerge(List<TreeNode> trees) {
        roots = new HashMap<>();
        for (TreeNode t : trees) {
            roots.put(t.val, t);
        }
        Set<Integer> leaves = new HashSet<>();
        for (TreeNode t : trees) {
            for (TreeNode child : new TreeNode[] {t.left, t.right}) {
                if (child != null) {
                    leaves.add(child.val);
                }
            }
        }
        List<TreeNode> top = new ArrayList<>();
        for (TreeNode t : trees) {
            if (!leaves.contains(t.val)) {
                top.add(t);
            }
        }
        if (top.size() != 1) {
            return null;  // no unique final root
        }
        TreeNode root = top.get(0);
        roots.remove(root.val);
        boolean ok = build(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
        return ok && roots.isEmpty() ? root : null;  // every tree must be used
    }

    // attach trees at leaves and check BST bounds
    private boolean build(TreeNode node, long lo, long hi) {
        if (node == null) {
            return true;
        }
        if (!(lo < node.val && node.val < hi)) {
            return false;
        }
        if (node.left == null && node.right == null && roots.containsKey(node.val)) {
            TreeNode sub = roots.remove(node.val);  // replace this leaf with its tree
            node.left = sub.left;
            node.right = sub.right;
        }
        return build(node.left, lo, node.val) && build(node.right, node.val, hi);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Root values are distinct and each leaf can take one tree, so the merge structure is forced; only the root is free.
  2. Checking bounds while attaching validates the whole merged tree in one pass.
  3. Leftover trees mean some couldn't be attached (or a cycle), so the answer is None.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Two trees attaching to each other (cycle) → None.
  • Already a single tree.
  • A merge that breaks BST order.

Complexity: O(n) time and space (each tree has at most 3 nodes).

Medium 1443. Minimum Time to Collect All Apples in a Tree Cisco Graph

Problem: Starting and ending at vertex 0, collect every apple in an undirected tree; each edge takes 1 second. Return the minimum time.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 7, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,4],[1,5],[2,3],[2,6]], hasApple = [false,false,true,false,true,true,false]
Output: 8
Explanation: The figure above represents the given tree where red vertices have an apple. One optimal path to collect all apples is shown by the green arrows.
Example 2
Input: n = 7, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,4],[1,5],[2,3],[2,6]], hasApple = [false,false,true,false,false,true,false]
Output: 6
Explanation: The figure above represents the given tree where red vertices have an apple. One optimal path to collect all apples is shown by the green arrows.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · edges.length == n - 1 · edges[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ ai < bi ≤ n - 1 · hasApple.length == n

Hint 1

Which edges must you walk?

Hint 2

Compute, bottom-up, whether each subtree has an apple and what collecting it costs.

From brute force to the pattern: Simulating walks is complicated; counting the needed edges is O(n).

Spot it: An edge must be walked (twice) exactly when the subtree below it holds an apple. That's a post-order DFS on the tree rooted at 0: each child reports its cost and whether it has an apple.

Why not another pattern? Simulating walks or trying orders is unnecessary; only which edges are used matters.

Approach:

  1. Root the tree at 0 (iteratively).
  2. Children first: cost[u] = Σ (cost[child] + 2) over children whose subtree has an apple.
  3. Return cost[0].
class Solution:
    def minTime(self, n: int, edges: List[List[int]], hasApple: List[bool]) -> int:
        adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b in edges:
            adj[a].append(b)
            adj[b].append(a)
        parent = [-1] * n
        order = [0]
        for u in order:
            for v in adj[u]:
                if v != parent[u]:
                    parent[v] = u
                    order.append(v)
        cost = [0] * n
        has = hasApple[:]  # does the subtree contain an apple?
        for u in reversed(order[1:]):  # children before parents
            if has[u]:
                p = parent[u]
                cost[p] += cost[u] + 2  # walk down to u and back
                has[p] = True
        return cost[0]
function minTime(n: number, edges: number[][], hasApple: boolean[]): number {
    const adj: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    for (const [a, b] of edges) {
        adj[a].push(b);
        adj[b].push(a);
    }
    const parent: number[] = new Array(n).fill(-1);
    const order: number[] = [0];
    for (let k = 0; k < order.length; k++) {
        const u = order[k];
        for (const v of adj[u]) {
            if (v !== parent[u]) {
                parent[v] = u;
                order.push(v);
            }
        }
    }
    const cost: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    const has = [...hasApple];  // does the subtree contain an apple?
    for (let k = order.length - 1; k >= 1; k--) {  // children before parents
        const u = order[k];
        if (has[u]) {
            const p = parent[u];
            cost[p] += cost[u] + 2;  // walk down to u and back
            has[p] = true;
        }
    }
    return cost[0];
}
class Solution {
    public int minTime(int n, int[][] edges, List<Boolean> hasApple) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        }
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
            adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]);
        }
        int[] parent = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(parent, -1);
        List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>(List.of(0));
        for (int k = 0; k < order.size(); k++) {
            int u = order.get(k);
            for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
                if (v != parent[u]) {
                    parent[v] = u;
                    order.add(v);
                }
            }
        }
        int[] cost = new int[n];
        boolean[] has = new boolean[n];  // does the subtree contain an apple?
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            has[i] = hasApple.get(i);
        }
        for (int k = order.size() - 1; k >= 1; k--) {  // children before parents
            int u = order.get(k);
            if (has[u]) {
                int p = parent[u];
                cost[p] += cost[u] + 2;  // walk down to u and back
                has[p] = true;
            }
        }
        return cost[0];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. An edge is needed iff the subtree below it contains an apple, and then it's walked once down and once back.
  2. Processing children before parents accumulates costs bottom-up.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No apples → 0.
  • Apple only at the root → 0.
  • Edges listed in any direction.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Hard 428. Serialize and Deserialize N-ary Tree Microsoft Apple StringStack

Problem: Design serialize(root) and deserialize(data) for an N-ary tree.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: root = [1,null,3,2,4,null,5,6]
Output: [1,null,3,2,4,null,5,6]
Explanation: Node 1 has children 3, 2, 4; node 3 has children 5, 6.
Example 2
Input: root = [1,null,2,3,4,5,null,null,6,7,null,8,null,9,10,null,null,11,null,12,null,13,null,null,14]
Output: [1,null,2,3,4,5,null,null,6,7,null,8,null,9,10,null,null,11,null,12,null,13,null,null,14]
Example 3
Input: root = []
Output: []

Constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10⁴] · 0 ≤ Node.val ≤ 10⁴ · The height of the n-ary tree is less than or equal to 1000 · Do not use class member/global/static variables to store states. Your encode and decode algorithms should be stateless

Hint 1

Preorder alone can't show where a node's children end.

Hint 2

Write the number of children after each value.

From brute force to the pattern: This is already linear; the design question is what to write so it can be decoded.

Spot it: A preorder traversal that writes each node's value and its number of children is enough to rebuild the tree: read a value and a count, then recursively read that many subtrees.

Why not another pattern? Writing only values loses the structure; null markers per possible child don't work when the number of children varies.

Approach:

  1. Serialize: val count then each child's serialization.
  2. Deserialize with an iterator: read val, count, build count children recursively.
class Codec:
    def serialize(self, root: "Node") -> str:
        out = []

        def write(node):
            out.append(str(node.val))
            out.append(str(len(node.children)))  # how many subtrees follow
            for child in node.children:
                write(child)

        if root:
            write(root)
        return " ".join(out)

    def deserialize(self, data: str) -> "Node":
        if not data:
            return None
        tokens = iter(data.split())

        def read():
            node = Node(int(next(tokens)), [])
            for _ in range(int(next(tokens))):
                node.children.append(read())  # exactly that many children
            return node

        return read()
class Codec {
    serialize(root: _Node | null): string {
        const out: string[] = [];

        function write(node: _Node): void {
            out.push(String(node.val));
            out.push(String(node.children.length));  // how many subtrees follow
            for (const child of node.children) {
                write(child);
            }
        }

        if (root !== null) {
            write(root);
        }
        return out.join(" ");
    }

    deserialize(data: string): _Node | null {
        if (data === "") {
            return null;
        }
        const tokens = data.split(" ");
        let position = 0;

        function read(): _Node {
            const node = new _Node(Number(tokens[position++]), []);
            const count = Number(tokens[position++]);
            for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
                node.children.push(read());  // exactly that many children
            }
            return node;
        }

        return read();
    }
}
class Codec {
    // Encodes a tree to a single string.
    public String serialize(Node root) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root != null) {
            write(root, out);
        }
        return String.join(" ", out);
    }

    private void write(Node node, List<String> out) {
        out.add(String.valueOf(node.val));
        out.add(String.valueOf(node.children.size()));  // how many subtrees follow
        for (Node child : node.children) {
            write(child, out);
        }
    }

    private String[] tokens;
    private int position;

    // Decodes your encoded data to tree.
    public Node deserialize(String data) {
        if (data.isEmpty()) {
            return null;
        }
        tokens = data.split(" ");
        position = 0;
        return read();
    }

    private Node read() {
        Node node = new Node(Integer.parseInt(tokens[position++]), new ArrayList<>());
        int count = Integer.parseInt(tokens[position++]);
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
            node.children.add(read());  // exactly that many children
        }
        return node;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The child count tells the reader exactly where each node's subtree list ends.
  2. An empty tree serializes to an empty string.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Empty tree.
  • A single node.
  • Wide nodes with many children.

Complexity: O(n) time and space for both directions.

Hard 2791. Count Paths That Can Form a Palindrome in a Tree Microsoft Hash Map

Problem: Count pairs u < v whose path's edge letters can be rearranged into a palindrome.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: parent = [-1,0,0,1,1,2], s = "acaabc"
Output: 8
Explanation: The valid pairs are: - All the pairs (0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (1,4) and (2,5) result in one character which is always a palindrome. - The pair (2,3) result in the string "aca" which is a palindrome. - The pair (1,5) result in the string "cac" which is a palindrome. - The pair (3,5) result in the string "acac" which can be rearranged into the palindrome "acca".
Example 2
Input: parent = [-1,0,0,0,0], s = "aaaaa"
Output: 10
Explanation: Any pair of nodes (u,v) where u < v is valid.

Constraints: n == parent.length == s.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ parent[i] ≤ n - 1 for all i ≥ 1 · parent[0] == -1 · parent represents a valid tree. · s consists of only lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

When can letters be rearranged into a palindrome?

Hint 2

Represent letter parities from the root as a bitmask; what is the mask of a u–v path?

From brute force to the pattern: All pairs with path walks are O(n²) or worse; masks + hash map are O(26n).

Spot it: A multiset forms a palindrome iff at most one letter has odd count. Store each node's parity mask from the root; the path's mask is mask[u] ^ mask[v] (the shared part cancels). Count earlier nodes with an equal mask or one bit off using a hash map.

Why not another pattern? Checking every pair of nodes is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Compute mask[v] = mask[parent] ^ bit(s[v]) in BFS order.
  2. For each node: add count[mask] and count[mask ^ (1 << b)] for each of 26 bits; then record its mask.
from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def countPalindromePaths(self, parent: List[int], s: str) -> int:
        n = len(parent)
        children = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for v in range(1, n):
            children[parent[v]].append(v)
        mask = [0] * n
        order = [0]
        for u in order:  # parents before children
            for v in children[u]:
                mask[v] = mask[u] ^ (1 << (ord(s[v]) - 97))  # letter parity from the root
                order.append(v)
        seen = Counter()
        pairs = 0
        for v in order:
            m = mask[v]
            pairs += seen[m]  # every letter even
            for b in range(26):
                pairs += seen[m ^ (1 << b)]  # exactly one odd letter
            seen[m] += 1
        return pairs
function countPalindromePaths(parent: number[], s: string): number {
    const n = parent.length;
    const children: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    for (let v = 1; v < n; v++) {
        children[parent[v]].push(v);
    }
    const mask: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    const order: number[] = [0];
    for (let k = 0; k < order.length; k++) {  // parents before children
        const u = order[k];
        for (const v of children[u]) {
            mask[v] = mask[u] ^ (1 << (s.charCodeAt(v) - 97));  // letter parity from the root
            order.push(v);
        }
    }
    const seen = new Map<number, number>();
    let pairs = 0;
    for (const v of order) {
        const m = mask[v];
        pairs += seen.get(m) ?? 0;  // every letter even
        for (let b = 0; b < 26; b++) {
            pairs += seen.get(m ^ (1 << b)) ?? 0;  // exactly one odd letter
        }
        seen.set(m, (seen.get(m) ?? 0) + 1);
    }
    return pairs;
}
class Solution {
    public long countPalindromePaths(List<Integer> parent, String s) {
        int n = parent.size();
        List<List<Integer>> children = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            children.add(new ArrayList<>());
        }
        for (int v = 1; v < n; v++) {
            children.get(parent.get(v)).add(v);
        }
        int[] mask = new int[n];
        List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>(List.of(0));
        for (int k = 0; k < order.size(); k++) {  // parents before children
            int u = order.get(k);
            for (int v : children.get(u)) {
                mask[v] = mask[u] ^ (1 << (s.charAt(v) - 'a'));  // letter parity from the root
                order.add(v);
            }
        }
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        long pairs = 0;
        for (int v : order) {
            int m = mask[v];
            pairs += seen.getOrDefault(m, 0);  // every letter even
            for (int b = 0; b < 26; b++) {
                pairs += seen.getOrDefault(m ^ (1 << b), 0);  // exactly one odd letter
            }
            seen.merge(m, 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        return pairs;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Edges above the meeting point appear on both root paths, so they cancel in the XOR.
  2. Counting before inserting counts each pair once.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All the same letter.
  • A single node → 0.
  • Deep chains.

Complexity: O(26 · n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 889. Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Postorder Traversal Apple Binary TreeHash Map

Problem: Rebuild any binary tree matching the given preorder and postorder traversals (distinct values).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: preorder = [1,2,4,5,3,6,7], postorder = [4,5,2,6,7,3,1]
Output: [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]
Example 2
Input: preorder = [1], postorder = [1]
Output: [1]

Constraints: 1 ≤ preorder.length ≤ 30 · 1 ≤ preorder[i] ≤ preorder.length · All the values of preorder are unique. · postorder.length == preorder.length · 1 ≤ postorder[i] ≤ postorder.length · All the values of postorder are unique. · It is guaranteed that preorder and postorder are the preorder traversal and postorder traversal of the same binary tree.

Hint 1

Where is the left subtree's root in preorder?

Hint 2

Where does that root appear in postorder, and what does that tell you?

From brute force to the pattern: Linear searches for split points make it O(n²); a position map makes it O(n).

Spot it: Like building from preorder + inorder: the root is pre[0]; the next value pre[1] roots the left subtree, and in postorder that root is the last value of the left subtree, so its index gives the subtree size. Recurse (divide and conquer) with a hash map of postorder positions.

Why not another pattern? Searching for the split position linearly each time is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. pos[v] = index of v in postorder.
  2. build(pre_lo, pre_hi, post_lo): root pre[pre_lo]; if more nodes, left_size = pos[pre[pre_lo + 1]] − post_lo + 1.
  3. Recurse for left and right parts.
class Solution:
    def constructFromPrePost(self, preorder: List[int], postorder: List[int]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(postorder)}

        def build(pre_lo, pre_hi, post_lo):  # preorder[pre_lo..pre_hi] starting at postorder[post_lo]
            if pre_lo > pre_hi:
                return None
            root = TreeNode(preorder[pre_lo])
            if pre_lo == pre_hi:
                return root
            left_root = preorder[pre_lo + 1]
            left_size = pos[left_root] - post_lo + 1  # left subtree ends at its root in postorder
            root.left = build(pre_lo + 1, pre_lo + left_size, post_lo)
            root.right = build(pre_lo + left_size + 1, pre_hi, post_lo + left_size)
            return root

        return build(0, len(preorder) - 1, 0)
function constructFromPrePost(preorder: number[], postorder: number[]): TreeNode | null {
    const pos = new Map<number, number>();
    postorder.forEach((v, i) => pos.set(v, i));

    // preorder[preLo..preHi] starting at postorder[postLo]
    function build(preLo: number, preHi: number, postLo: number): TreeNode | null {
        if (preLo > preHi) {
            return null;
        }
        const root = new TreeNode(preorder[preLo]);
        if (preLo === preHi) {
            return root;
        }
        const leftRoot = preorder[preLo + 1];
        const leftSize = pos.get(leftRoot)! - postLo + 1;  // left subtree ends at its root in postorder
        root.left = build(preLo + 1, preLo + leftSize, postLo);
        root.right = build(preLo + leftSize + 1, preHi, postLo + leftSize);
        return root;
    }

    return build(0, preorder.length - 1, 0);
}
class Solution {
    private Map<Integer, Integer> pos;
    private int[] preorder;

    public TreeNode constructFromPrePost(int[] preorder, int[] postorder) {
        pos = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < postorder.length; i++) {
            pos.put(postorder[i], i);
        }
        this.preorder = preorder;
        return build(0, preorder.length - 1, 0);
    }

    // preorder[preLo..preHi] starting at postorder[postLo]
    private TreeNode build(int preLo, int preHi, int postLo) {
        if (preLo > preHi) {
            return null;
        }
        TreeNode root = new TreeNode(preorder[preLo]);
        if (preLo == preHi) {
            return root;
        }
        int leftRoot = preorder[preLo + 1];
        int leftSize = pos.get(leftRoot) - postLo + 1;  // left subtree ends at its root in postorder
        root.left = build(preLo + 1, preLo + leftSize, postLo);
        root.right = build(preLo + leftSize + 1, preHi, postLo + leftSize);
        return root;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. In postorder a subtree's root comes last, so the left child's index ends the left block.
  2. When a node has a single child, preorder and postorder can't tell left from right; treating it as left is accepted (any valid tree).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • A single node.
  • Nodes with one child (ambiguous).
  • A full binary tree.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.
